items.title: Dave Rivello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012
items.q: for 16th or 32nd note things in Coltrane or something you had a chance at getting those notes

ctx.x: That’s a good answer. In fact, you lead me to a question about analyzing things to death. This one article I read recently that I’m sort of obsessing about. It’s a five plus page article in the latest JazzEd magazine about playing, if you had Dm7 to Bflat7, and the possibilities. And this article goes on and on and on for five pages, and there’s a matrix and a whole schematic. And for a guy like me, who basically didn’t get a jazz education so to speak, I found that I could hardly read it. I mean do you have an…

The way I think about that is when you are a young musician it’s important because jazz was handed down. It was an aural tradition. So I think that when you’re younger it’s very important to transcribe the masters, and as much as possible get those notes off of the recording without using the technology we have today where there’s some things you can just play it in and it actually writes it out for you. No. You take it note for note. You know we used to, there was the Marantz tape decks that would run at half…

That’s the next thing that’s going to happen is somebody learning to improvise. Stuff’s going to come out in the wrong order. But over time and as you continue to listen and you continue to assimilate, eventually the sentences start to come out in the right order. But it’s necessary to listen and to transcribe and to do that work yourself. It’s not the same — you know even when I was a kid there weren’t ten thousand jazz books. There were a few things. Jamey Abersold only had — I told a student at Eastman the…
